errata.was: New Testament chronology dates its documents; this article tests one of them as an ancestor. It proposes a literary-genealogical test for the priority question: a literature proposed as earliest should exhibit recoverable ancestry, its load-bearing forms derivable from independently attested antecedents, while the forms that follow it may show transformations of it. On that test the received sequence is anomalous: it begins with the literature whose immediate Christian ancestry must be reconstructed, as the field's own category 'pre-Pauline' concedes, and ends with the literature whose ancestry can be read.
errata.now: Johannes Sigil and Damascus Dancings test one document of the New Testament's chronology as the ancestor of the rest. Their test for the priority question is literary-genealogical: the literature put forward as earliest should show recoverable ancestry, its load-bearing forms derivable from antecedents attested independently, and what comes after it may show transformations of it. By that test the received sequence is anomalous. It starts with the literature whose Christian ancestry has to be reconstructed, as the field's own category 'pre-Pauline' concedes, and ends with the literature whose ancestry can be read.
